name: AWS Chalice
summary: A Flask-style Python framework for AWS Lambda: decorators turn functions into API routes and event handlers, and one `chalice deploy` creates the functions, API and IAM policy.
intro: A Chalice app is a Python file with an `app = Chalice(app_name=...)` object and decorated functions. `@app.route("/orders/{id}")` adds a REST endpoint behind Amazon API Gateway; `@app.schedule`, `@app.on_s3_event`, `@app.on_sqs_message` and similar decorators connect a function to a timer, a bucket, a queue or a topic, and there are WebSocket handlers, authorizers (IAM, Cognito or your own function), blueprints for splitting an app across files, and middleware. All routes share one Lambda function, `api_handler`; each event handler gets its own. `chalice local` serves the routes on your machine for quick testing.

Deployment is part of the framework. `chalice deploy` packages your code and the dependencies in `requirements.txt`, calls the AWS APIs through the Python SDK to create or update the Lambda functions, API and event sources, and records what it made per stage in `.chalice/deployed/<stage>.json`. By default it reads your code to generate the IAM policy the functions need; you can turn that off and supply your own. For CloudFormation-based pipelines, `chalice package` writes a SAM template and a `deployment.zip` instead, `--pkg-format terraform` writes a Terraform file, and the `chalice.cdk` construct embeds an app in an AWS CDK stack. A given app must stick to one route: switching between `chalice deploy` and a packaged deployment creates a second set of resources.

Chalice is an AWS open-source project under Apache 2.0. Releases have slowed to roughly one a year (1.32.0 in May 2025, 1.33.0 in May 2026, adding Python 3.14), but the repository is still active: in October 2026 it gained Python 3.15 and arm64 support that had not yet been released.
strengths: Very little to learn for Python developers: Flask-like routes plus decorators for AWS events, and the README promises a deployed API in under 30 seconds
One command deploys everything, including an IAM policy generated from the AWS calls in your code
Can hand off to SAM, Terraform or the CDK when the app needs to join a larger infrastructure-as-code setup
Maintained by AWS and still on 1.x since 2017, under a promise of backward compatibility within each major version
limits: AWS Lambda and Python only; there is no way to target another cloud or runtime
Its own docs say the feature set is purposely small and it restricts how an app is structured and deployed
Releases are now infrequent, one in the year to May 2026, and mostly track Python versions rather than add features
Resources created by `chalice deploy` live outside CloudFormation, so moving to `chalice package` later means a fresh set of resources

story: On July 11, 2016 the AWS Developer Tools team released a preview of the Python Serverless Microframework for AWS, soon known by its package name, Chalice. Its programming model copied Flask, which the team picked for its reputation for simplicity, and its goal was to minimize the time to a working API: one `chalice deploy` packaged the code, created the Lambda function and API Gateway resources and returned a URL. It lived in the awslabs organization and was explicitly not yet meant for production.

Chalice 1.0.0 became generally available on July 31, 2017, with a promise of backward compatibility within each major version. By then it handled dependencies with C extensions, pure Lambda functions, scheduled events, generated IAM policies, authorizers and CI pipelines. Later releases added WebSockets and Terraform packaging (1.10, 2019), built-in support for the AWS CDK (1.22, 2021) and CDK v2 (1.27, 2022).

After that the pace slowed to maintenance: new Python versions as Lambda adds them, old ones dropped, and dependency updates. The project, now under the aws organization on GitHub, is still maintained in 2026 but adds few new features.

choices.why: Flask was already familiar to many Python developers, so routes and handlers needed little explanation and the framework stayed small.

choices.choice: Deploy with the SDK, not CloudFormation
choices.why: Calling the AWS APIs directly kept the tool self-contained: no template to write or stack to manage. CloudFormation, Terraform and CDK output were added later for teams that need them.

choices.choice: Generate the IAM policy from the code
choices.why: Writing least-privilege policies by hand is a common stumbling block; analysing the AWS calls the app makes produced a starting policy automatically.

choices.choice: One Lambda function for all routes
choices.why: Every API request goes to a single `api_handler` function, and Chalice dispatches it to the right view inside, so the whole API deploys as one unit; event handlers get functions of their own.
